paragraphs.text: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyposis and mucocutaneous melanin pigmentation, with melanin spots of the lips, buccal mucosa, and digits (Dormandy, 1957; Giardiello et al., 1987; Hemminki et al., 1997; Jenne et al., 1998). Patients have a markedly elevated risk of malignancy, including gastrointestinal cancer and extraintestinal cancers such as those of the breast, ovary, testis, and uterine cervix (Hemminki et al., 1997; Mehenni et al., 1997). Hemminki et al. (1998) described PJS as a rare hereditary disease that predisposes to benign and malignant tumors in many organ systems.

paragraphs.text: Cantu et al. (1980) described a 6-year-old boy with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and a unilateral feminizing Sertoli cell tumor. Endocrinologic studies showed consistently high plasma and urine estrogen levels with normal testosterone and dihydrotestosterone levels. The raised estrogen levels did not change with exogenous gonadotropin administration, indicating autonomous production. Histology of the nontumorous testicular tissue suggested that estrogens may have had both stimulating and atrophying effects on the seminiferous tubules. The authors concluded that gonadal tumors are an additional manifestation of the PJS gene in both male and female patients.
